subtitles.text: When you log in to your bank, your password travels through many machines you don't control.
With plain H T T P, it travels like an open book. Anyone along the road can read it.
H T T P S fixes that. It's the same H T T P, wrapped in a protocol called T L S.
T L S gives you three things: privacy, proof that nothing was changed, and proof of who you're talking to.
It starts with a handshake. Steve says hello to the bank, and the bank says hello back.
Then the bank shows its certificate, a name tag that says mybank dot com.
Anyone can write a name tag, so this one is stamped by a certificate authority, a cleric that Steve's browser already trusts.
The bank also proves it holds the secret key that matches the tag. A thief with a copy of the tag can't do that.
Now they need a shared secret, but the road is full of eyes. So they mix colors.
They agree on a public color, yellow. Everyone can see it.
Steve adds his secret red and sends orange. The bank adds its secret blue and sends green.
The spy on the road sees yellow, orange and green. Never red, never blue.
Steve adds his red to the bank's green. The bank adds its blue to Steve's orange.
Both end up with the same brown. The spy can't unmix the paint, so he can't make it.
That brown becomes the key. From now on, every message travels in a chest locked with it.
The spy sees boxes going back and forth, and nothing inside.
And if anyone tampers with a box, the seal breaks and the message is thrown away.
All of that happens in milliseconds, and your browser shows it as a padlock.
But careful. The padlock means the line is private and the name checks out, not that the site is honest.
A fake bank at my b four n k dot com can get a padlock too. So read the name.
That's H T T P S. A handshake, a stamped name tag, some paint, and locked chests all the way.
